t.3.1: Autumn has arrived like a young bride, lovely in form: robed in kāśa grass, her charming face the open lotuses, delightful with the jingling of anklets that is the cry of passion-maddened geese, her slender body gracefully bowed like the ripening rice.
t.3.2: The earth is whitened by kāśa grasses, the nights by the cool-rayed moon, the waters of the rivers by swans, the lakes by white water-lilies, the forest edges by saptacchada trees bowed with their burden of blossoms, and the groves by mālatī jasmines.
t.3.3: Their girdles are lovely darting śapharī fish, their necklaces the rows of white birds settled along their banks, their round hips the broad edges of their sandbanks: the rivers now move slowly, like passionate young women.
t.3.4: Here and there the sky, with clouds white as silver, conch-shell and lotus-fibre, which have shed their water and drift by the hundreds in their lightness, tossed by the force of the wind, looks like a king being fanned with hundreds of yak-tail whisks.
t.3.5: The sky, lovely with the lustre of a mass of crushed collyrium, the earth reddened by the pollen of bandhūka flowers, and the fields whose stretches of ground are covered with ripened kalama rice: whose young man's heart on earth do they not fill with longing?
t.3.7: Wearing the hosts of stars as her finest ornaments, her moon-face freed from the veil of clouds, and clad in the spotless silken garment of moonlight, the night grows fuller day by day, like a young girl ripening into womanhood.
t.3.6: Its lovely branch-tips tossed by the gentle breeze, its tender shoots crowned with clusters of opening blossoms, its flowing nectar drunk by intoxicated bees, whose heart does the kovidāra not rend?
t.3.8: The rivers, their garlands of ripples jostled by the beaks of kāraṇḍava ducks, their banks crowded with flocks of kādamba geese and sārasa cranes, reddened with the pollen of lotuses, bring delight to people all around with the cries of the haṃsas.
t.3.10: Shaking the fields of rice bowed low beneath the weight of their grain, setting the noble trees, bent with blossoms, to dancing, and tossing the lotus pool with its groves of full-blown lotuses, the wind forcibly stirs the hearts of the young.
t.3.9: The moon, a festival for the eyes, wreathed in a garland of heart-ravishing rays, delightful and showering cool drops of spray, burns all the more fiercely the bodies of women who have been wounded by arrows seared with the poison of separation from their husbands.
t.3.11: Adorned by pairs of passion-maddened haṃsas, decked with clear, full-blown kamala and utpala lotuses, and wreathed in rows of ripples stirred up by the gentle breeze of dawn, the lakes suddenly fill the heart with yearning.
t.3.12: The bow of Balabhid has vanished into the bellies of the clouds, and today the lightning, the banner of the sky, flickers no more. The cranes no longer fan the heavens with the breeze of their wings, and the peacocks no longer gaze at the sky with upturned faces.
t.3.13: Leaving the peacocks, now without their practice of dancing, Madana goes to the sweetly singing haṃsas; and the splendor of fresh blossoming, abandoning the kadamba, kuṭaja, arjuna, sarja and nīpa trees, has passed to the saptacchadas.
t.3.14: The groves, charming with the fragrance of śephālikā blossoms, echoing with flocks of birds perched at ease, and having for their blue lotuses the eyes of does standing along their borders, fill the hearts of men with longing.
t.3.15: Again and again shaking the white water-lilies, lotuses and night-blooming lilies, and grown far colder from their touch, the wind at daybreak, stirred by the dewdrops clinging to the tips of the leaves, fills the heart with intense longing.
t.3.16: The lands along the village bounds, their ground covered with heaps of ripened rice, adorned with abundant herds of cattle resting at ease, and echoing with the cries of geese joined by flocks of sārasa cranes, fill the hearts of men with delight.
t.3.17: The swans have outdone the graceful gait of women, the blooming lotuses the moonlike loveliness of their faces, the blue water-lilies their eyes languid with passion, and the delicate ripples the charming play of their brows.
t.3.18: The dark creepers, their shoots bowed beneath the weight of blossoms, steal the beauty of women's arms adorned with ornaments; and the fresh mālatī, lovely with kaṅkeli flowers, steals the moonlike radiance of their bright smiles, lit by the gleam of their teeth.
t.3.19: Women fill their exceedingly thick, dark, curly-tipped tresses with fresh jasmine blossoms, and in their ears, adorned with the finest golden earrings, they set blue lotuses of many kinds.
t.3.20: Today women, their hearts filled with delight, adorn the round orbs of their breasts with necklaces and moist sandal paste, the very broad slopes of their hips with clusters of girdle-strings, and their lotus-feet with the finest sweetly tinkling anklets.
t.3.21: The cloudless sky, strewn with the moon and stars, bears the surpassing beauty of the lakes, which are filled with blossoming lilies, sheltered by royal swans, and adorned with water that gleams like emerald gems.
t.3.23: Some other young women, charming with their lotus-like hands, their hands clasped in their lovers' hands, their faces outshining the moon, abandon their delight in song and music and, driven by overpowering desire, mostly go home to a chamber fragrant with arranged flowers.
t.3.22: In autumn the winds blow cool from their contact with the water lilies; the quarters of the sky, rid of their masses of clouds, are lovely; the water is free of turbidity, the earth has its mud dried, and the sky, with its moon of spotless rays, is studded with stars.
t.3.25: At daybreak today the lotus, touched by the rays of the sun, opens wide, resembling the face of a lovely young woman; and the night-lily too closes as the moon's disc sinks to its setting, like the smile of wives when their beloved husbands have gone abroad.
t.3.24: In autumn, young beloved women, playful with the delight of love-making and joined by their dear friends, openly betray the sport of the five-arrowed god of love; with the incomparable flush upon their faces, they reveal their pastimes and joys in the middle of the night.
t.3.26: Seeing in the blue lotuses the beauty of their beloveds' dark eyes, in the cries of the impassioned geese the jingling of their golden girdles, and in the bandhujīva flower the lovely radiance of their lips, the travellers now weep, their minds bewildered.
t.3.27: Leaving the moon's loveliness in the faces of women, the sweet call of the haṃsa in their jewelled anklets, and the glow of the bandhūka flower in their captivating lips, the gracious splendour of autumn's coming departs to some unknown place.
t.3.28: Her face a blooming lotus, her eyes full-blown blue water-lilies, wearing a white garment of freshly opened kāśa grass, lovely in her radiance like the white night-lotus, may this Autumn, like a passion-intoxicated woman, bestow the highest delight upon your hearts.
